source_text: Tawnr igitur ostensiones cum sint, non oportet adhuc quzerere apud alios yeritatem, quam facile est ab Ecclesia sumere ; cum Apostoli, quasi in depositorium dives, plenissime in eam contulerint omnia que sint veritatis: uti omnis quicunque velit, sumat ex ea potum vitee. Hee est enim vitze introitus; omnes autem reliqui fures sunt et latrones. Propter quod oportet devitare quidem illos; que autem sunt Ecclesiz, cum summa diligentia diligere, et apprehendere veritatis traditionem. Quid enim? Et si de aliqua modica queestione disceptatio esset, nonne oporteret in antiquissimas recurrere ecclesias, in quibus Apostoli conversati sunt, et ab eis de presenti quastione sumere quod certum et re liquidum est? Quid autem si neque Apostoli quidem Scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportebat ordinem sequi_ traditionis, quam tradiderunt iis quibus committebant ecclesias? Cui ordinationi assentiunt multze gentes barbarorum eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine charta vel atramento scriptam habentes per Spiritum in cordibus suis salutem, et veterem traditionem diligenter custodientes, in unum Deum credentes fabricatorem cceli et terree, et omnium quz in eis sunt, per Christum Jesum Dei Filium. Qui propter eminentissimam erga figmentum suum dilectionem, eam que esset ex Virgine generationem sustinuit, ipse per se hominem adunans Deo, et passus sub Pontio Pilato, et resurgens, et in claritate receptus, in gloria venturus Salvator eorum qui salvantur, et judex eorum qui judicantur, et mittens in ignem sternum transfiguratores veritatis, et contemtores Patris sui et adventus ejus. Hane fidem qui sine literis crediderunt, quantum ad sermonem nostrum, barbari sunt: quantum autem ad sententiam, et consuetudinem, et conversationem, propter fidem perquam sapientissimi sunt, et placent Deo, conversantes in omni justitia et castitate et sapientia. Quibus si aliquis annuntiaverit ea que ab hereticis adinventa sunt, proprio sermone eorum colloquens, statim concludentes aures longo longius fugient, ne audire quidem sustinentes blasphemum colloquium. | Sie per illam veterem stolorum traditionem, ne in conceptionem quidem mentis admittunt, quodcunque eorum portentiloquium est, neque enim congregatio fuit apud eos, neque doctrina instituta. 2. Ante Valentinum enim non fuerunt, qui sunt a Valentino; neque ante Marcionem erant, qui sunt a Marcione; neque omnino erant reliqui sensus maligni, quos supra enumeravimus, initiatores et inventores perversitatis eorum fierent. Valentinus enim venit Romam sub Hygino; Pio, et prorogavit tempus usque ad Anicetum. Oerdon autem qui ante Marcionem, et hic sub Hygino, qui fuit octavus episcopus, seepe in ecclesiam veniens, et exhomologesin faciens, sic consummavit, modo quidem latenter docens, modo vero exhomologesin faciens, modo vero ab aliquibus traductus in his que docebat male, et abstentus est a religiosorum hominum conventu. 3. Marcion autem illi succedens invaluit sub Aniceto, !}decimum locum episcopatus continente. Reliqui vero qui vocantur Gnostici, a Menandro Simonis discipulo, quemadmodum ostendimus, accipientes initia, unusquisque eorum, cujus participatus est sententiz, ejus et pater, et antistes apparuit. Omnes autem hi multo posterius, mediantibus jam Ecclesize temporibus, insurrexerunt in suam apostasiam.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, since these are demonstrations, it is not necessary to seek truth from others, which is easy to take from the Church; since the Apostles, as if into a rich repository, have fully conferred all things of truth into it: so that anyone who wishes may take from it the drink of life. For this is the entrance of life; all the rest, however, are thieves and robbers. On account of which it is necessary to avoid them; but those things which are of the Church, with the greatest diligence to love and to seize the tradition of truth. For what? And if there were a dispute about some small question, would it not be necessary to recur to the most ancient churches, in which the Apostles conversed, and from them to take concerning the present question what is certain and clear? But what if even the Apostles had not left us Scriptures, would it not be necessary to follow the order of tradition, which they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the churches? To which ordination many barbarian nations, who believe in Christ, assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit without paper or ink, and diligently preserving the old tradition, believing in one God, the maker of heaven and earth, and all things that are in them, through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Who, on account of his most excellent love towards his creature, sustained the generation which was from the Virgin, himself gathering man to God, and having suffered under Pontius Pilate, and having risen, and having been received in glory, is to come in glory as the Savior of those who are saved, and the judge of those who are judged, and sending into eternal fire those who transfigure truth, and contemners of his Father and his advent. These who have believed without letters, as far as our speech is concerned, are barbarians: but as far as judgment, and custom, and conversation are concerned, on account of faith they are most wise, and pleasing to God, living in all justice, and chastity, and wisdom. To whom if anyone should announce those things which have been invented by heretics, speaking in their own language, immediately closing their ears, they will flee far, far away, not even enduring to hear the blasphemous conversation. Thus, through that old tradition of the elders, they do not even admit into their conception of mind whatever their portentous speech is, nor was there a gathering among them, nor a doctrine instituted. For before Valentinus, those who are from Valentinus were not; nor before Marcion, were those who are from Marcion; nor were there at all the remaining malignant senses, which we enumerated above, to become the initiators and inventors of their perversity. For Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus; and Pius, and prolonged his time until Anicetus. But Cerdo, who was before Marcion, and this under Hyginus, who was the eighth bishop, often coming into the church, and making a confession, thus consummated, sometimes teaching secretly, sometimes making a confession, sometimes being led astray by some in those things which he taught badly, and was absent from the gathering of religious men. And Marcion, succeeding him, grew strong under Anicetus, holding the tenth place of the episcopate. But the rest, who are called Gnostics, taking their beginnings from Menander, the disciple of Simon, as we have shown, each one of them, whose sentiment he has participated in, has appeared as his father, and high priest. But all these, much later, with the times of the Church intervening, have risen up into their own apostasy.
pass_b_english: Since these demonstrations exist, we no longer need to seek the truth from others, for it is readily available from the Church; the Apostles deposited every truth into it as if into a rich treasury, so that anyone who desires may draw from it the water of life (John 4:14; Rev 21:6). This is the entrance to life; all the rest are thieves and robbers (John 10:1, 8). Therefore we must avoid them, while loving and clinging with the utmost diligence to what belongs to the Church and to the tradition of truth (2 Thess 2:15). If even a minor dispute arose, would we not turn to the most ancient churches where the Apostles lived, and receive from them a clear and certain answer on the matter at hand? And if the Apostles had left us no Scriptures, would it not still be necessary to follow the order of tradition they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the churches? (2 Tim 2:2)

Many nations of barbarians who believe in Christ assent to that order. They possess salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit without paper or ink (Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3), carefully preserving the ancient tradition. They believe in one God, the maker of heaven and earth and all that is in them (Gen 1:1; Acts 14:15), through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Because of his surpassing love for his creation, he endured being born of the Virgin, himself uniting humanity to God; he suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose again, was received in glory, and will come in glory as the Savior of the saved and the Judge of the judged (Acts 10:42; 2 Tim 4:1), sending into eternal fire those who distort the truth and despise his Father and his coming (Matt 25:41; 2 Pet 2:1).

Those who have believed without written documents are, as far as our language goes, barbarians; yet in judgment, custom, and conduct they are supremely wise because of their faith, and they please God, living in all righteousness, chastity, and wisdom (Jas 3:13; Titus 2:12). If anyone announces to them the inventions of heretics, speaking in their own tongue, they instantly stop their ears and flee far away, refusing even to hear the blasphemous talk. Thus, through that ancient tradition of the elders, they do not even admit such portentous speech into their minds, for there was no assembly among them and no instituted doctrine (cf. 1 Cor 14:33). Before Valentinus, those from Valentinus did not exist; before Marcion, those from Marcion did not exist; nor did the other malignant teachings we enumerated above exist as the initiators and inventors of their perversity.

Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, continued under Pius, and remained until Anicetus. Cerdo, who preceded Marcion, appeared under Hyginus, the eighth bishop. He often entered the Church and made confession, but ended by sometimes teaching secretly, sometimes confessing, sometimes being corrected by others for teaching badly, and finally withdrawing from the assembly of the godly. Marcion succeeded him and flourished under Anicetus, who held the tenth place in the episcopate. The rest, called Gnostics, received their beginnings from Menander, the disciple of Simon, as we have shown; each one became the father and high priest of the opinion he adopted. All these arose much later, in the midst of the Church's era, rising up into their own apostasy (1 Tim 4:1; 2 Tim 3:13).

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal translation, and Pass B provides a fluent version with appropriate scriptural citations for the allusions present in the Latin (e.g., 'vitæ potum' to John 4:14). All clauses, including the historical details regarding the succession of bishops (Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus) and the origins of the various heresies, are preserved.
